case_title: Prosecutor v. Naser Orić — superior responsibility for detention crimes
question: Has it been established beyond reasonable doubt that the commander of the Srebrenica armed forces was criminally responsible as a superior, under Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute, for failing to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the murder and cruel treatment of Serb detainees in Srebrenica between 27 December 1992 and 20 March 1993?
facts: Between September 1992 and March 1993, Serbs were detained in Srebrenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the police station and at a building behind the Srebrenica Municipal Building. The Trial Chamber found that crimes of murder and cruel treatment were committed against the detainees during two periods: from 24 September to 16 October 1992, and from 15 December 1992 to 20 March 1993. It found that the Military Police was responsible for the occurrence of all these crimes, and that the Military Police was subordinated to the commander of the Srebrenica armed forces, through the successive Chiefs of Staff, only after 27 November 1992. The persons who physically committed the crimes were not found to be members of the Military Police or to be directly subordinated to the commander. The head of the Military Police after 27 November 1992 was found to be subordinated to the commander and responsible for the crimes committed between December 1992 and March 1993. The Trial Chamber's findings on the commander's mental state concerned his knowledge of, or reason to know of, the crimes committed in the two detention facilities. The Trial Chamber convicted him under Article 7(3) for failing to prevent the murder and cruel treatment committed between 27 December 1992 and 20 March 1993, and sentenced him to two years' imprisonment.
holding: In its Judgement of 3 July 2008, the ICTY Appeals Chamber reversed the convictions and acquitted the accused of all charges. The Trial Chamber had identified only one culpable subordinate, the head of the Military Police, but had failed to resolve whether and on what basis that subordinate incurred criminal responsibility, and had failed to make a finding on whether the accused knew or had reason to know that this subordinate was about to engage, or had engaged, in criminal conduct. Without these findings the convictions under Article 7(3) could not stand. The Prosecution's alternative basis, superior responsibility for unidentified guards, had not been pleaded in the Indictment.

verdict.conclusion: Yes. The commander's criminal responsibility under Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute for failing to prevent the murder and cruel treatment of Serb detainees between 27 December 1992 and 20 March 1993 has been established beyond reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber's factual findings — that the Military Police was subordinated to the commander through the Chiefs of Staff after 27 November 1992, that the head of the Military Police was responsible for the crimes during the charged period, and that the commander knew or had reason to know of the abuses yet failed to take necessary and reasonable measures — satisfy each element of superior responsibility: effective authority and control, knowledge (actual or constructive), and culpable omission. No objections were raised to challenge these arguments. The conviction rests on corroborated evidence linking the commander to the command structure and to the failure to act, leaving no reasonable alternative explanation. The legal standards in customary IHL (Rule 153), Additional Protocol I (Article 86(2)), and the Rome Statute (Article 28) — which reflect the same principles as Article 7(3) ICTY — are met on these facts. The standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt is satisfied by the Chamber's determinations. The sentence of two years' imprisonment reflects the gravity of the omission. arguments.claim: The commander exercised effective authority and control over the Military Police during the period 27 December 1992 – 20 March 1993, satisfying the control element of command responsibility.
arguments.reasoning: Customary rule 153 establishes that a superior who has effective authority and control over subordinates is liable for their crimes. The factual record shows that the Military Police was subordinated to the commander through the Chiefs of Staff after 27 November 1992, creating a direct chain of command. Article 86(2) of Additional Protocol I reinforces that such a superior relationship imposes responsibility when the superior has the power to prevent or repress breaches. Accordingly, the commander possessed the legal authority to direct, supervise, and discipline the Military Police, meeting the control requirement of Article 7(3) ICTY.

citations.quoted_text: Commanders and other superiors are criminally responsible for war crimes committed by their subordinates if they knew, or had reason to know, that the subordinates were about to commit or were committing such crimes and did not take all necessary and reasonable measures in their power to prevent their commission, or if such crimes had been committed, to punish the persons responsible.

The fact that a breach of the Conventions or of this Protocol was committed by a subordinate does not absolve his superiors from penal or disciplinary responsibility, as the case may be, if they knew, or had information which should have enabled them to conclude in the circumstances at the time, that he was committing or was going to commit such a breach and if they did not take all feasible measures within their power to prevent or repress the breach.

arguments.claim: The commander failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures within his power to prevent or repress the murders and cruel treatment, thereby breaching his duty under Article 7(3) ICTY.
arguments.reasoning: Article 28(a)(ii) of the Rome Statute obliges a commander to take all necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or repress the commission of crimes, or to refer them to competent authorities. The factual record shows that no effective orders, investigations, or disciplinary actions were undertaken by the commander after becoming aware of the abuses. Both the Rome Statute provision and customary rule 153 require such measures; the commander’s inaction constitutes the requisite omission for command responsibility.

citations.quoted_text: That military commander or person failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures within his or her power to prevent or repress their commission or to submit the matter to the competent authorities for investigation and prosecution.
...and did not take all necessary and reasonable measures in their power to prevent their commission, or if such crimes had been committed, to punish the persons responsible.

citation.quoted_text: That military commander or person failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures within his or her power to prevent or repress their commission or to submit the matter to the competent authorities for investigation and prosecution.
...and did not take all necessary and reasonable measures in their power to prevent their commission, or if such crimes had been committed, to punish the persons responsible.

arguments.claim: Taken together, the established control, knowledge, and omission satisfy the elements of Article 7(3) ICTY, and the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt is met by the Trial Chamber’s findings.
arguments.reasoning: The Tribunal’s factual findings confirm the commander’s authority over the Military Police, his knowledge (or constructive knowledge) of the crimes, and his failure to act. Under the legal standards set out in the Rome Statute, customary IHL, and Additional Protocol I, these facts fulfill each element of superior criminal responsibility. The standard of proof required—beyond reasonable doubt—is satisfied because the Chamber’s determinations are based on corroborated evidence linking the commander to the control structure and to the omission, leaving no reasonable alternative explanation.
